text: A modern traction elevator doesn't hang from one rope. It hangs from several steel ropes, often four to eight, and any one of them could hold the loaded car. They run over a grooved wheel at the top, down to a counterweight that balances the car, so the motor barely has to lift. The motor has its own brake, held open by electricity. If the power goes off, springs clamp it shut, and the car just stays where it is. And a separate system watches the speed. A thin rope loops from the car, up around a wheel called the governor, and back down. As the car moves, the governor spins. If it spins too fast, weights inside swing outward, and trip a clamp that grabs the governor rope. That yanks a lever on the car, which jams steel wedges against the guide rails. The car squeezes to a stop. And at the very bottom of the shaft, buffers, big springs or oil pistons, soften any last landing.
